vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW

root_cause.description: read() is called with a size argument of 0x100 (256 bytes) but writes into a stack buffer at rbp-0x70 that is only 0x70 (112) bytes long. There is no bounds check on the read size relative to the buffer capacity. The read size (0x100) exceeds the buffer size (0x70) by 144 bytes, allowing the attacker to overwrite the stack canary (at rbp-0x8, 104 bytes from buffer start), saved rbp (at rbp+0, 112 bytes from buffer start), and return address (at rbp+0x8, 120 bytes from buffer start).

data_flow: read() writes up to 256 bytes into echo_buf at rbp-0x70 (112-byte buffer)
bytes 0-103 fill echo_buf up to canary boundary
bytes 112-119 overwrite saved rbp at rbp+0
bytes 120-127 overwrite return address at rbp+0x8
bytes 128-255 overwrite further stack beyond return address

security_check.expected: read() size argument should not exceed the destination buffer size (0x70 = 112 bytes), or a bounds check should limit the read to the buffer capacity
security_check.actual: read() is called with size=0x100 (256 bytes) into a 112-byte buffer with no size validation
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: No bounds check between the read size (0x100) and the buffer capacity (0x70). The size argument to read() is a hardcoded constant 0x100 that is larger than the buffer.

vulnerable_operation.target: stack buffer at rbp-0x70 (112 bytes) and beyond (canary, saved rbp, return address)

impact.reason: The overflow writes past the 112-byte buffer boundary, corrupting the stack canary (at offset 104), saved rbp (at offset 112), and return address (at offset 120). The canary check at 0x12c2-0x12d1 will detect canary corruption and call __stack_chk_fail, but the memory corruption itself occurs before the check. If combined with BUG-002 (canary leak), the canary can be preserved during overflow.
The overflow overwrites saved rbp and return address on the stack, corrupting control flow data.

evidence.description: lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; mov edx,0x100; mov rsi,rax; mov edi,0x0; call read@plt — read() is called with buffer at rbp-0x70 and size=0x100 (256 bytes)
add rsp,0xffffffffffffff80 — stack frame is 0x80 (128) bytes; echo_buf at rbp-0x70 spans 112 bytes to rbp-0x8 where canary is stored
Buffer at rbp-0x70 is 112 bytes (0x70). read() writes 0x100 (256) bytes. Overflow of 144 bytes covers canary (offset 104), saved rbp (offset 112), return address (offset 120), and 136 bytes beyond.
Canary check: mov rcx,[rbp-0x8]; sub rcx,fs:0x28; je 0x12d6; call __stack_chk_fail — canary is checked before return, but overflow has already corrupted memory

verification_required: Confirm that read() returns the full input length when attacker sends > 112 bytes
Confirm that __stack_chk_fail is triggered when canary is overwritten (canary protection is active)
Confirm whether BUG-002 canary leak can be combined with BUG-001 to bypass canary protection

vulnerabilities.title: STACK_INFO_LEAK_VIA_PRINTF

root_cause.description: After read() fills the echo buffer, the code only null-terminates the buffer if the byte at buf[read_retval] equals 0x0a (newline). This check examines the byte at index read_retval (one past the last byte actually read), not the last byte read itself. If the attacker sends input without a trailing newline, or fills the buffer to a specific length where buf[read_retval] is not 0x0a, the buffer is not null-terminated. The subsequent printf("%s", buf) call then reads past the 112-byte buffer boundary as an unbounded string, leaking stack data including the canary value at rbp-0x8 (104 bytes from buffer start).

attack_surface.input: stdin via read(0, rbp-0x70, 0x100), echoed via printf("%s", rbp-0x70)
data_flow: stdin -> read(0, rbp-0x70, 0x100) at 0x1248, returns N bytes
read_retval (N) stored as DWORD at rbp-0x7c
buf[N] = byte at [rbp+N-0x70] is loaded at 0x1255
if buf[N] == 0x0a, buf[N] is set to 0x00 at 0x1263 (null-termination)
printf("%s", rbp-0x70) at 0x127b reads unbounded string from buffer
without null-terminator, printf reads past 112-byte buffer into canary and beyond

security_check.expected: The echo buffer should always be null-terminated before being passed to printf("%s"), regardless of input content
security_check.actual: Null-termination only occurs if buf[read_retval] (the byte after the last read byte) happens to be 0x0a (newline). If the attacker controls input length and content to avoid this condition, the buffer remains non-null-terminated.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: The null-termination logic is conditional on the stack residue byte at buf[read_retval] being 0x0a. There is no unconditional null-termination of the buffer. The check should null-terminate buf[read_retval-1] (the last byte read) or buf[read_retval] unconditionally.

vulnerable_operation.target: stack buffer at rbp-0x70 and beyond (canary at rbp-0x8, saved rbp, return address)

impact.reason: If the buffer is not null-terminated, printf("%s") reads past the 112-byte buffer boundary and outputs stack data to stdout. The canary at rbp-0x8 (104 bytes from buffer start) can be leaked. This info leak can be used to bypass the stack canary protection that guards BUG-001.

evidence.description: mov eax,[rbp-0x7c]; cdqe; movzx eax,BYTE[rbp+rax-0x70]; cmp al,0xa; jne 0x1268; mov BYTE[rbp+rax-0x70],0x0 — null-termination is conditional: only if buf[read_retval]==0x0a
lea rax,[rbp-0x70]; mov rsi,rax; lea rdi,'%s'; call printf@plt — printf("%s") is called on the buffer which may not be null-terminated

The check examines buf[read_retval], which is the byte at index N (one past the last byte read by read()). This byte is stack residue, not attacker-controlled input. If it is not 0x0a, no null-termination occurs, and printf reads past the buffer into the canary region.

Canary is at rbp-0x8, which is 104 bytes (0x68) from buffer start at rbp-0x70. If attacker sends exactly 104 bytes without trailing newline, buf[104] is the canary's first byte. If that byte is not 0x0a, printf reads through the canary and outputs it, leaking the canary value.

verification_required: Confirm that stack residue at buf[read_retval] is not 0x0a when attacker sends specific input lengths
Confirm that printf output includes the canary bytes when buffer is not null-terminated
Confirm the exact input length needed to leak the canary (likely 104 bytes to reach canary boundary)
Verify whether the loop allows multiple leak attempts (continue_flag initialized to 'N', loop continues until 'Y'/'y')

non_vulnerabilities.description: init() at 0x1195 calls setvbuf(stdin/stdout/stderr, 0, _IONBF, 0) and alarm(60). No user input is processed. setvbuf parameters are correct (mode 2 = _IONBF, unbuffered). alarm(60) sets a 60-second timeout but is not a vulnerability.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: No attacker-controlled data flows through init(). All parameters are hardcoded constants. setvbuf usage is correct.

non_vulnerabilities.description: scanf("%7s", rbp-0x78) reads the Y/N continue flag with a 7-character limit into an 8-byte slot at rbp-0x78.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The %7s format specifier limits input to 7 characters plus null terminator (8 bytes total), which fits exactly in the 8-byte slot at rbp-0x78. No overflow occurs from this input path. The continue_flag slot is above the echo buffer (rbp-0x78 < rbp-0x70) and does not overlap.

non_vulnerabilities.description: The cdqe instruction at 0x1253 sign-extends the 32-bit read return value to 64-bit. If read() returns -1 (error), cdqe produces 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, causing buf[-1] access.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: This is an error path that requires read() to fail (e.g., stdin closed). Under normal operation with an open stdin, read() returns >= 0. This is a minor robustness issue, not a primary vulnerability. The main vulnerabilities are the buffer overflow (BUG-001) and info leak (BUG-002).

unresolved.description: Whether the printf info leak (BUG-002) can reliably leak the full 8-byte canary value
unresolved.reason: The leak depends on stack residue at buf[read_retval] not being 0x0a, and on there being no null bytes in the stack data between the buffer end and the canary. The canary typically has a null byte as its least significant byte (glibc design), which would stop printf before leaking the remaining canary bytes.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic verification: send specific input lengths (e.g., 104, 105, 112 bytes) and observe printf output to determine if canary bytes are leaked. Check if the canary's null byte (LSB) truncates the leak.

unresolved.description: Whether the canary's null LSB can be bypassed to leak the full canary
unresolved.reason: Glibc stack canaries have a null byte as the least significant byte to prevent string-based leaks. If printf stops at this null byte, only the null byte itself is leaked (confirming canary presence) but not the remaining 7 bytes. The attacker may need to leak byte-by-byte by sending increasing input lengths.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic verification: test byte-by-byte leak strategy by sending inputs of length 105, 106, ..., 111 to see if each additional byte of the canary can be leaked individually.

unresolved.description: Whether the alarm(60) timeout affects the feasibility of multi-step leak+overflow attacks
unresolved.reason: The 60-second alarm will SIGALRM-terminate the process. If the canary leak requires multiple loop iterations (byte-by-byte), the time constraint may limit the number of leak attempts.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic verification: measure time per loop iteration and calculate how many leak iterations fit within 60 seconds.
